docs.title: Tournament Management System
docs.text:
TMS runs the robot game side of a FIRST LEGO League event from one small server on your local network. Referees score on tablets, the head referee runs matches and the timer, the audience watches a live scoreboard, and nothing depends on an internet connection.

Legacy branch

This documentation describes the legacy TMS codebase, which is receiving maintenance and season updates only. New development happens on the rebuild.

docs.title: What TMS does
docs.text:
• Digital scoring with season scoresheets that validate answers and calculate the score for the referee.
  • Live schedules for matches and judging sessions, imported from a schedule file and editable during the day.
  • Match control with a shared match timer, start and end sounds, and table ready signals.
  • Live rankings on a public scoreboard that updates as scores arrive.
  • Integrity checks that flag missing scores, conflicting scores and schedule clashes while the event is running.
  • Automatic backups with one-click restore.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text: TMS backs up the whole event automatically and lets you restore any backup with a couple of clicks. Backups are managed on the Backups page, in the side menu. Only an admin can open it.

docs.title: What a backup contains
docs.text:
Everything: teams, tables, matches, scoresheets, judging sessions, pods, users and settings. A backup is a complete snapshot of the event at one moment.

Backups are stored as .zip files in the backups folder next to the server program. The file name includes the date and time it was taken.

docs.title: Automatic backups
docs.text:
The server takes a backup on a timer. Both settings are in Setup → System Setup.

Setting Default Meaning Backup interval 10 minutes How often a backup is taken Backups to retain 5 How many are kept before the oldest is deleted. 0 keeps them all.

With the defaults you can always go back to a point within the last ten minutes, and as far back as roughly fifty minutes.

Event day settings

Disk space is not a concern for an event of this size. Setting backups to retain to 0 on the day keeps every backup, so you can go back to any point in the event.

docs.title: Manual backups
docs.text:
Select Create Backup to take one immediately. Do this:

  • once setup is complete, as your clean starting point,
  • before importing a schedule into an event that already has data,
  • before restoring or purging, and
  • at the end of the event.

docs.title: Downloading a backup
docs.text: Each backup in the list has a download button. Use it to keep a copy somewhere other than the server computer, such as a USB stick. Do this at least at the end of the event.

docs.title: Restoring a backup
docs.text:
Restoring replaces the entire current state of the event with the backup.

  1. Create a backup first, so you can return to where you are now.
  2. Find the backup you want in the list and select Restore.
  3. Confirm.

Every connected device updates to the restored state.

Restoring overwrites the current event

Everything entered since the chosen backup was taken is lost: scoresheets, schedule edits, check-ins. Only restore when that is what you intend.

The server may stop during a restore

The Backups page carries a caution for a reason. If a backup file is damaged, the database can fail while loading it and the server will stop. If that happens, start the server again and restore a different backup.

flowchart TD
    A[Something has gone badly wrong] --> B[Create a backup of the current state]
    B --> C[Restore the last good backup]
    C --> D{Event looks right?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Re-enter anything recorded since that backup]
    D -- No --> F[Restore an older backup, or the one from step B]
    F --> D

docs.title: Moving an event to another computer
docs.text:
1. On the old server, create a backup and download it.
  2. Install TMS on the new computer and start it.
  3. Stop the new server, copy the backup file into its backups folder, and start it again.
  4. Log in as admin (with the default password, since this is a new server) and restore the backup from the Backups page.

After the restore, the accounts and passwords are those of the original event.

Note

Restore through the Backups page instead of copying the tms.kvdb folder between machines. The server checks the data as it loads it.

docs.title: If the server computer fails
docs.text: The backups are on the server computer, so a dead disk takes them with it. For an event that matters, download a backup to another device at natural breaks, such as lunch and the end of each round. With that file and a spare laptop you can be running again in a few minutes using the steps above.

docs.title: Event setup
docs.text:
The Setup page holds every event-wide setting. Only an admin can open it.

Each row has a send button at its right-hand end. A setting is not saved until you press the button on its row, and a short message confirms the result. All settings can be changed while the event is running, and take effect on every device straight away.

docs.title: Event name
docs.text: A name for the event. Optional.

docs.title: Admin password
docs.text:
Sets the password of the admin account. Change it from the default admin before the event.

Danger

Whoever has the admin password can change scores, restore backups and purge the event.

docs.title: Backup interval
docs.text: How often the server takes an automatic backup, in minutes. The default is 10.

docs.title: Backups to retain
docs.text:
How many backups the server keeps. When the limit is reached the oldest is deleted to make room. The default is 5. Setting 0 keeps every backup.

See Backups and restore.

docs.title: Upload schedule
docs.text: Choose the schedule CSV file, then press send. See Schedules for where the file comes from and what the import creates.

docs.title: Select Blueprint
docs.text:
Chooses the scoresheet referees use.

  • A season, such as 2026-Founders, gives referees the full scoresheet for that game with automatic scoring and checks.
  • Agnostic gives referees a single score box.

See Seasons and games.

docs.title: Timer length
docs.text: The length of a match in seconds. The default is 150 (2:30).

docs.title: Endgame length
docs.text:
How many seconds before the end of the match the end-game phase begins, when the clock changes colour and the end-game sound plays. The default is 30.

See Match timer.

docs.title: Purge
docs.text:
PURGE empties the whole database: teams, matches, tables, scoresheets, judging sessions and pods, and also the user accounts and the settings on this page. The server returns to the state of a fresh install, with only the admin account and its default password. You are asked to confirm.

Use it to clear a test event before the real one, or to start again after importing the wrong schedule.

This cannot be undone

Create a backup first, on the Backups page. A backup is the only way back.

docs.title: Recommended setup order
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Admin password] --> B[Event name]
    B --> C[Upload schedule]
    C --> D[Select blueprint]
    D --> E[Create users]
    E --> F[Check Dashboard]
  1. Change the admin password.
  2. Set the event name.
  3. Upload the schedule.
  4. Select the blueprint.
  5. Create user accounts.
  6. Open the Dashboard and resolve any integrity messages.
  7. Create a manual backup. This is your clean starting point.

docs.title: Installing the server
docs.text: The TMS server is one program plus a folder of web files. It needs no database server, no installer and no internet connection once it is on the machine.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A laptop or small computer that stays on for the whole event. Any modern machine is more than enough.
  • A place on the venue network that the other devices can reach. See Network planning.

docs.title: Choose how to run it
docs.text:
WindowsLinuxmacOSDocker
  1. Download the Windows build from the releases page.
  2. Unzip it to a folder you can find again, for example C:\TMS.
  3. Double-click tms_server.exe, or run it from a terminal opened in that folder.

The first time, Windows Firewall asks whether to allow network access. Allow it for the network you are on, otherwise other devices cannot connect.

  1. Download the Linux build from the releases page.
  2. Unpack the archive and start the server from inside the unpacked folder:
cd tms
./tms_server
  1. Download the macOS build from the releases page.
  2. Unpack it and start the server from a terminal inside the folder:
cd tms
./tms_server

If macOS blocks the program because it was downloaded from the internet, allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

docker pull cjbuchel/tms
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name tms cjbuchel/tms

The event data lives inside the container. To keep it across container upgrades, mount a volume for the working folder:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 \
  -v tms-data:/tms/tms.kvdb \
  -v tms-backups:/tms/backups \
  --name tms cjbuchel/tms

Always start the server from its own folder

The server looks for its web files, log settings and database relative to the folder it is started in. Starting it from somewhere else will fail or create a second, empty event.

docs.title: Check it is running
docs.text:
When the server starts it prints a line like:

Hosting on http://192.168.1.20:8080

Open that address in a browser on another device. You should see the TMS home screen. Then follow the quick start.

docs.title: What is in the server folder
docs.text: Item What it is tms_server The server program tms_client/ The web client that the server hosts at /ui log_config/ Settings for what is written to the logs tms.kvdb/ The event database. Created on first run. Do not edit or delete it while the server is running. backups/ Automatic and manual backups, as .zip files logs/ Log files. See Logs and files. cert.pem, key.rsa The certificate and key used when the server runs with --tls

docs.title: Starting a new event
docs.text:
Each server folder holds one event. For a new event, either:

  • unpack a fresh copy of TMS into a new folder, or
  • log in as admin and use Purge in Setup to empty the current one.

Keeping one folder per event means you always have the complete record of past events.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
1. Stop the server.
  2. Take a copy of the whole server folder.
  3. Unpack the new version into a new folder.
  4. Copy your backups folder across, start the new server, and restore the most recent backup from the Backups page.

Restoring through the server, instead of copying the tms.kvdb folder by hand, lets the new version check the data as it loads.

docs.title: Stopping the server
docs.text: Close the terminal window or press Ctrl+C in it. Everything is saved as it happens, so there is nothing to save first.

docs.title: Network planning
docs.text: TMS needs one thing from the network: every device must be able to reach the server computer. Most event-day problems are network problems, so it is worth ten minutes of planning.

docs.title: The simple, reliable setup
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    router[Dedicated Wi-Fi router, not connected to the internet]
    server[TMS server laptop, wired]
    router --- server
    router -.- t1[Referee tablets]
    router -.- t2[Head referee and emcee]
    router -.- t3[Judge advisor]
    router --- d1[Scoreboard and timer computers, wired if possible]
  • Bring your own router. Venue Wi-Fi is often configured so that devices cannot see each other, which stops TMS working.
  • Wire the server to the router with a cable. Wire the display computers too if you can.
  • Use a network name and password only your volunteers have.
  • The router does not need an internet connection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Detail Reachability Every device must be able to open a connection to the server's address and port Port TCP 8080 by default, or whatever you set with --port Protocols HTTP and WebSocket on that one port, or HTTPS and secure WebSocket with --tls Internet Not required Bandwidth Very low. A scoresheet is a few kilobytes.

docs.title: Give the server a fixed address
docs.text:
Devices find the server by its IP address. If that address changes during the day, every device loses the server.

Do one of the following:

  • In the router's settings, reserve an address for the server computer (often called a DHCP reservation or static lease).
  • Or set a static IP address on the server computer, outside the range the router hands out.

Then write the address on a card for each volunteer, or show the QR code from the connection page.

docs.title: Firewalls
docs.text:
The server computer must accept incoming connections on its port.

WindowsmacOSLinux

Allow tms_server.exe when Windows Firewall asks on first run. If you dismissed the prompt, open Windows Security → Firewall & network protection → Allow an app through firewall and tick TMS for the network type you are on.

Set the network to Private in Windows network settings. Windows blocks most incoming connections on networks marked Public.

If the firewall is on, allow incoming connections for tms_server in System Settings → Network → Firewall → Options.

If you use ufw:

sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp

docs.title: Using venue Wi-Fi
docs.text:
If you must use the venue's network, test it beforehand. Ask the venue's IT contact two questions:

  1. Is client isolation turned on? If it is, devices cannot reach each other and TMS will not work on that network.
  2. Can a device keep the same address all day?

A quick test: start the server on one device and open its address from a phone on the same Wi-Fi. If the home screen loads, the network is usable.

If the network is shared with the public, run the server with --tls and change every default password.

docs.title: Keep the server awake
docs.text:
Before the event, on the server computer:

  • Plug in the power supply.
  • Turn off sleep and hibernate, including when the lid closes.
  • Pause automatic updates and restarts for the day.
  • Close anything else that might use the same port.

docs.title: Devices that sleep
docs.text:
Tablets drop their connection when they sleep and reconnect when they wake. This is normal: the connection markers appear in the top bar for a moment and then clear. Nothing is lost.

If a device does not reconnect within a few seconds, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Reaching TMS from outside the venue
docs.text: By default TMS is only reachable on the local network. To let people off-site view the scoreboard, see Remote access.

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text:
Normally TMS can only be reached from the venue network. Remote access publishes your server at a public web address, so people who are not at the venue can open it, for example parents watching the scoreboard or a remote scorekeeper.

It works through the tms.mobi relay service. Your server makes an outgoing connection to the relay, and the relay forwards visitors to it. You do not need to open ports on the venue's router.

flowchart LR
    visitor[Visitor on the internet] -->|"yourevent.tms.mobi"| relay[tms.mobi relay]
    relay <-->|outgoing tunnel| server[TMS server at the venue]
    local[Devices at the venue] <--> server

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An internet connection on the server computer.
  • A token for the relay service, issued by the TMS maintainers. Without a token the relay will not accept your server.
  • A subdomain name for your event, for example curtin.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Start the server with both options:

./tms_server --proxy_token YOUR_TOKEN --proxy_domain curtin

The first time, the server downloads a small helper program (frpc) that runs the tunnel. This needs internet access and takes a few seconds. When the tunnel is up, the server log shows:

Tunnel active: https://curtin.tms.mobi

Your event is then available at that address, over HTTPS. Devices at the venue can keep using the local address as before.

Note

Both options are required. If only the token is given, the server logs a warning and starts without the tunnel.

docs.title: If the tunnel drops
docs.text: The server keeps trying to reconnect on its own. Devices on the local network are not affected at all: remote access is an extra path in, not something the event depends on.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Publishing your server makes it reachable by anyone who knows or guesses the address.

Before you turn on remote access

  • Change the admin password.
  • Change the passwords of every default account, or delete the ones you do not use.
  • Treat the token like a password. Do not share it or commit it to a repository.

Visitors who do not log in can only see the public screens: the scoreboard and the timer. Everything else needs an account.

docs.title: When not to use it
docs.text:
• If the venue's internet is unreliable. A tunnel that keeps dropping only confuses people.
  • If nobody off-site needs access. A closed local network is simpler and more private.
  • For referee tablets at the venue. They should always use the local address, so that scoring never depends on the internet.

docs.title: Server options
docs.text:
The server takes its options on the command line. With no options it listens on every network interface on port 8080 without encryption, which suits most events.

./tms_server --help

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning --addr <ADDR> 0.0.0.0 The address to listen on. 0.0.0.0 means every network interface. --port <PORT> 8080 The port to listen on. --tls off Serve over HTTPS and secure WebSockets instead of HTTP. --cert <PATH> cert.pem The certificate file to use with --tls. --key <PATH> key.rsa The private key file to use with --tls. --proxy_token <TOKEN> none Token for the tms.mobi remote access service. --proxy_domain <NAME> none Subdomain to publish the server on, for example curtin for curtin.tms.mobi. -h, --help Print the options and exit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
DefaultDifferent portEncryptedYour own certificate 
./tms_server

Reachable at http://<server address>:8080.

./tms_server --port 80

Port 80 is the default web port, so people can type just the server's address. On Linux and macOS, ports below 1024 need administrator rights.

./tms_server --tls

Reachable at https://<server address>:8080.

./tms_server --tls --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem

docs.title: Encryption (TLS)
docs.text:
By default TMS does not encrypt traffic. On a closed event network this is the most compatible choice: every browser and tablet connects without warnings.

Turn on --tls when the network is shared with people you do not trust, such as open venue Wi-Fi.

docs.title: How certificates are chosen
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Server starts with --tls"] --> B{"--cert and --key given?"}
    B -- Yes --> C{Both files exist?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Use them]
    C -- No --> F[Generate a self-signed certificate for this run only]
    B -- No --> E{cert.pem and key.rsa exist in the server folder?}
    E -- Yes --> D
    E -- No --> G[Generate a self-signed certificate for this machine]
    G --> H[Save it as cert.pem and key.rsa for next time]

docs.title: Self-signed certificates and browser warnings
docs.text:
A certificate the server generates for itself is not issued by a recognised authority, so browsers show a warning the first time each device connects. On each device, choose to continue to the site.

To avoid the warning you need a certificate that devices already trust, which in practice means a real domain name. For most events it is simpler to run without --tls on a private network, or to use remote access, which provides HTTPS for you.

Note

The clients try HTTPS first and fall back to HTTP, so they work with either setting without being reconfigured.

docs.title: Running as a service
docs.text:
For a permanent installation you may want the server to start with the machine.

Linux (systemd)Docker /etc/systemd/system/tms.service
[Unit]
Description=TMS server
After=network-online.target

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/opt/tms
ExecStart=/opt/tms/tms_server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl enable --now tms

docker run -d --restart unless-stopped -p 8080:8080 --name tms cjbuchel/tms

WorkingDirectory matters: the server must start in its own folder.

docs.title: Users and passwords
docs.text: Accounts are managed on the Users page, in the side menu. Only an admin can open it.

docs.title: The accounts you start with
docs.text:
A new server has one account you can log in with.

Username Password Role admin admin Admin

Change the admin password in Setup before doing anything else.

There is also a built-in public account with no password. It is what a device uses before anyone logs in, and it can only see the public screens. You do not log in to it.

docs.title: Default users
docs.text:
Add default users creates one shared account for each common role. Each account's password is the same as its username.

Username Password Role head_referee head_referee Head referee referee referee Referee judge_advisor judge_advisor Judge advisor judge judge Judge

This is the quickest way to get an event running: every referee tablet logs in as referee. Change the passwords if the network is not private.

docs.title: Adding a user
docs.text:
1. Select Add User.
  2. Enter a username and password.
  3. Tick the roles the account should have.
  4. Confirm.

The roles you can give are Admin, Queuer, Head Referee, Referee, Judge Advisor, Judge and Emcee. What each one can do is listed in Roles at a glance.

An account can have several roles. Remember that some roles include others: a head referee can already do everything a referee and queuer can, and a judge advisor everything a judge can.

docs.title: Editing and removing users
docs.text:
• The pencil on a row opens Edit User, where you can change the password and roles.
  • The bin on a row deletes the account, after a confirmation.

Changes apply the next time that account logs in. A device that is already logged in keeps working until it logs out or reconnects.

docs.title: Shared or personal accounts?
docs.text:
Shared accounts One account per role, for example every referee uses referee. Simple, quick, and enough for most events. The referee's name is still recorded on each scoresheet, because referees type it into the scoring screen. Personal accounts One account per person. Useful when you want to know which account corrected a scoresheet, or want to be able to remove one person's access.

A common middle ground is shared accounts for referees and queuers, and personal accounts for the head referee, judge advisor and admins.

docs.title: Password advice
docs.text:
Use event-only passwords

TMS is designed for a local event network, not as a secure identity system. Passwords are stored by the server as entered and are not protected against someone with access to the server computer. Never use a password here that anyone uses anywhere else.

  • Change the admin password.
  • If the network is shared with the public, change the default account passwords too and run the server with --tls.
  • After the event, there is nothing to clean up: accounts live in that event's database.

docs.title: Adding a season
docs.text:
A season is one Rust file in tms_infra/src/infra/fll_infra/seasons/. It defines the missions, the questions and their points, the rules that link answers together, and the validation checks.

Use the most recent season file as your starting point.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Create fll_<year>.rs in the seasons folder with a struct that implements BaseSeason.
  2. Register the module in seasons/mod.rs.
  3. Add the season to the SEASONS list in fll_blueprint_map.rs.
  4. Add mission images to tms_client/assets/images/missions/<year>/ and list the folder in tms_client/pubspec.yaml.
  5. Add tests in tms_infra/tests/fll_scoring.rs.
  6. Run ./run_codegen and rebuild the client.

docs.title: The season trait
docs.text:
pub trait BaseSeason {
  fn validate(&self, answers: &HashMap<String, QuestionAnswer>) -> Vec<QuestionValidationError>;
  fn get_season(&self) -> String;
  fn get_fll_game(&self) -> FllBlueprint;
}
get_season The name shown in the season dropdown and stored on every scoresheet. Once events have used it, do not change it. get_fll_game Returns the missions and questions. validate Returns a list of problems with a set of answers. An empty list means the sheet can be submitted.

docs.title: Missions and questions
docs.text:
Mission {
  id: "m01".to_string(),
  label: "M01 - Drone Survey".to_string(),
  image_url: None, // (1)!
},
  1. With None, the client looks for assets/images/missions/<season>/<mission id>.png. Set a path here to override it, which is how the two 2026 games share one image folder.

A question belongs to the mission whose id it starts with: m01a and m01b both belong to m01.

Question {
  id: "m01a".to_string(),
  label: "Is the drone no longer touching the mat?".to_string(),
  label_short: "Drone flown?".to_string(),
  input: QuestionInput::Categorical(CategoricalQuestion {
    options: vec![
      CategoricalOption { label: "No".to_string(), score: 0 },
      CategoricalOption { label: "Yes".to_string(), score: 20 },
    ],
    default_option: "No".to_string(),
  }),
  rules: vec![],
},

Every question is categorical: a fixed list of options, each worth a number of points, and a default. A number range is a list of options labelled 0, 1, 2 and so on. The client shows a list of more than eight consecutive numbers as a counter.

Choose defaults carefully

Defaults should describe a robot that never left base. A model that scores for being undisturbed defaults to yes; precision tokens default to all remaining. The test suite checks that the defaults pass validation.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
A rule replaces a question's score when its condition is true. Use rules for points that depend on another answer.

Question {
  id: "m01b".to_string(),
  // ...options: No = 0, Yes = 0
  rules: vec![QuestionRule {
    condition: "m01a == Yes && m01b == Yes".to_string(), // (1)!
    output: 10,
  }],
},
  1. The bonus is worth 10, but only when the main objective was also achieved.

How rules are evaluated:

  • A question id in a condition is replaced by that question's current answer.
  • The first rule whose condition is true wins, and its output replaces the option's score. If no rule matches, the option's own score is used.
  • Supported operators are ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, joined with && and ||. && binds tighter than ||.

Limits of the rule engine

  • Comparisons are made on text, not numbers. > and < are only reliable for single digits. For larger ranges, write one rule per value or do the work in validate.
  • A value in a condition must be a single word. An option labelled Mine dock cannot be matched; label it Mine.
  • Avoid parentheses. Write a == Yes && b == Yes || c == Yes && d == Yes and rely on && binding tighter.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
validate is ordinary Rust, so anything the rule engine cannot express goes here.

let released = number(answers, "m02a") + if is_yes(answers, "m09c") { 1 } else { 0 };
let planted = number(answers, "m14a");

if planted > released {
  errors.push(QuestionValidationError {
    question_ids: "m14a".to_string(), // (1)!
    message: format!("Seeds in replantation station {} exceeds max possible {}", planted, released),
  });
}
  1. The message is shown under this question on the scoresheet. Use a comma-separated list to attach it to several.

A sheet with any validation error cannot be submitted, on the client or the server. Only add a check when the answers are genuinely impossible, not merely unusual.

docs.title: Scoring and validation are separate
docs.text:
Remember that rules and validation do different jobs:

Rules Validation Changes the score Yes No Blocks submission No Yes Written as Condition strings Rust

A bonus that needs a prerequisite usually wants both: a rule so the bonus scores nothing without it, and a validation message so the referee notices.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Add a test for the new season in tms_infra/tests/fll_scoring.rs. The helpers there start from the season's defaults and apply the answers you give:

#[test]
fn my_new_season() {
  assert_eq!(score("2027", &[]), 50); // defaults
  assert_eq!(score("2027", &[("m01a", "Yes")]), 70);
  assert_eq!(score("2027", &[("m01b", "Yes")]), 50); // bonus without the objective
  assert_eq!(n_errors("2027", &[("m01b", "Yes")]), 1);
}

Cover every rule, every validation check, and the maximum possible score. Run them with:

cargo test -p tms_infra

The existing tests also check, for every season, that the default answers are valid and that every question belongs to a mission.

docs.title: A season with more than one game
docs.text: If a season has more than one game, add one struct per game in the same file and register each under its own name, as 2026-Founders and 2026-Future are. Prefix the image files (fo_m01.png, fu_m01.png) and set image_url on each mission so both games can share a folder.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page is for people working on TMS itself. It explains what the parts are and how data moves between them.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Folder Language What it is tms_server Rust The server: HTTP and WebSocket API, match and timer services, integrity checks, backups tms_infra Rust Shared data types, season scoresheets and the scoring rule engine. Used by the server directly and by the client through a bridge. tms_schedule_handler Rust Schedule CSV parser echo_tree_rs Rust EchoTree: the embedded database and its live-sync protocol echo_tree_infra Rust EchoTree protocol types and the schema generator echo_tree_flutter Dart EchoTree client for Flutter tms_client Dart (Flutter) The client application for web, iOS and Android docs Markdown This documentation .github/workflows YAML Build and release pipeline, and the documentation build

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph client [tms_client, Flutter]
        ui[Views and providers]
        bridge[Generated bridge]
        etf[echo_tree_flutter]
    end
    subgraph infra [tms_infra, Rust]

    end

docs.title: One codebase for scoring
docs.text:
The scoresheets and scoring rules live in tms_infra, in Rust, and are used in two places:

  • the server calls them directly to validate and score every submitted sheet, and
  • the client calls the same code through flutter_rust_bridge, compiled to WebAssembly for the web client and to a native library for iOS and Android.

So a score shown on a tablet and the score stored by the server come from the same code. There is no second implementation to keep in step.

flowchart LR
    src[tms_infra Rust source] --> native[Native library]
    src --> wasm[WebAssembly module]
    src --> srv[Linked into tms_server]
    native --> mobile[iOS and Android client]
    wasm --> web[Web client]

The bridge is fully synchronous (default_dart_async: false in tms_client/flutter_rust_bridge.yaml). That is a deliberate choice: synchronous calls need no worker threads, so the WebAssembly build needs no cross-origin isolation headers and works over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Three channels between client and server
docs.text:
Channel Used for Direction HTTP requests Commands: log in, submit a scoresheet, load a match, change a setting Client to server TMS WebSocket (/ws/<id>) Events: timer ticks, match loaded and ready, table signals Server to client EchoTree WebSocket (/echo_tree/ws/<id>) Data: the live copy of teams, matches, scores and so on Both ways

A client registers over HTTP first and receives an id and token. It sends those as the X-Client-Id and X-Auth-Token headers on every request.

docs.title: EchoTree
docs.text:
EchoTree is a small key-value database (built on sled) with a subscription protocol on top.

  • Data is organised into named trees, for example :teams or :robot_game:matches.
  • Each tree has a JSON schema, generated from the Rust types, and every write is validated against it.
  • Roles control which trees an account may read and write.
  • A client subscribes to the trees a screen needs. The server sends the current contents, then every change as it happens. The client keeps a local copy, so screens read from memory.

This is why the UI needs no refresh: views are built on providers that listen to their trees.

docs.title: A scoresheet's journey
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Referee tablet
    participant B as Bridge (wasm or native)
    participant S as tms_server
    participant D as EchoTree
    participant C as Other clients
    R->>B: calculate_score and validate, on every answer
    B-->>R: score and validation errors
    R->>S: POST submit_score_sheet
    S->>S: validate and recalculate with tms_infra
    S->>D: insert scoresheet
    S->>D: recalculate rankings
    D-->>C: scoresheet and team changes
    D-->>R: same changes

docs.title: Server services
docs.text: Match service Holds which matches are loaded and ready, runs the timer, and publishes timer and match events to every client. When the timer finishes it marks the loaded matches complete. Integrity service Re-checks the event data on a schedule and writes its findings to the integrity messages tree, which the Dashboard and other screens subscribe to. Backup service Takes a backup on the configured interval and prunes old ones.

docs.title: Client structure
docs.text:
Folder in tms_client/lib Contents views One folder per screen widgets Shared widgets, including the scoresheet renderer providers State, one provider per area of data, built on EchoTree subscriptions services HTTP calls to the server network Connection handling: HTTP, WebSocket, EchoTree, and the connectivity state shown in the top bar generated Bridge code generated from tms_infra. Never edit by hand.

Routing is in lib/router.dart. Which screens a role sees is decided in two places that must agree: the client (home screen and side menu) and the server (the role filter on each route).

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Version Used for Rust Current stable Server and shared code Rust 1.99.0 Pinned in tms_infra/rust-toolchain.toml Client native library and WebAssembly builds. rustup installs it automatically. Flutter 3.47.7 Client flutter_rust_bridge_codegen 2.13.0 Generating the Dart bindings wasm-pack Current Building the WebAssembly module 
cargo install flutter_rust_bridge_codegen --version 2.13.0
cargo install wasm-pack

Why two Rust versions?

The Flutter build hook that compiles tms_infra for mobile requires an exact, pinned toolchain so that builds are reproducible. The pin only applies to commands run from inside tms_infra. The server builds from the workspace root on your normal stable toolchain.

docs.title: Quick build
docs.text:
# 1. generate the bridge code and build the wasm module
./run_codegen

# 2. build the web client
cd tms_client
flutter build web
cd ..

# 3. run the server, which hosts tms_client/build/web
cargo run -p tms_server

Then open http://localhost:8080.

docs.title: What run_codegen does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[tms_infra Rust source] -->|flutter_rust_bridge_codegen generate| B[Dart bindings in tms_client/lib/generated]
    A -->|generate| C[Rust glue in tms_infra/src/frb_generated.rs]
    B -->|build_runner, run automatically| D[freezed classes]
    A -->|wasm-pack build --release| E[tms_client/web/pkg]
  1. flutter_rust_bridge_codegen generate reads tms_infra and writes the Dart bindings and the Rust glue. It also runs build_runner for the generated freezed classes, so there is no separate step for that.
  2. wasm-pack build compiles tms_infra to WebAssembly for the web client.

Run it whenever you change anything in tms_infra that the client can see: a data type, a season, or a function.

Why not flutter_rust_bridge_codegen build-web?

That command builds a threaded WebAssembly module, which needs a nightly toolchain and cross-origin isolation headers. TMS's bridge is fully synchronous and never uses threads, so a plain stable wasm-pack build is all it needs. The result is smaller and works over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Building each part
docs.text:
ServerWeb clientAndroidiOSDocker 
cargo build -p tms_server --release

The binary is target/release/tms_server. It expects to be run from a folder that contains log_config and tms_client/build/web. From the repository root that is already true.

./run_codegen
cd tms_client && flutter build web

Output is tms_client/build/web, which the server hosts at /ui.

cd tms_client && flutter build apk

The Rust library is compiled for each Android ABI by the build hook in tms_client/hook/build.dart. The Android NDK is required.

cd tms_client && flutter build ipa

Requires macOS and Xcode. The same build hook compiles the Rust library.

The Dockerfile packages a prebuilt Linux (musl) server binary with the web client. Build those first, then:

docker build -t tms .

docs.title: How the Rust library reaches the client
docs.text:
Native platforms use Flutter's native assets: tms_client/hook/build.dart tells Flutter to build the crate at ../tms_infra and bundle the result into the app. There is no separate plugin package and nothing to run by hand.

The web client loads the WebAssembly module from web/pkg, which run_codegen produces.

docs.title: Developing
docs.text:
Run the server, then run the client with hot reload against it:

cargo run -p tms_server

cd tms_client
flutter run -d chrome

A client started this way is not hosted by the server, so use its connection page to point it at localhost and port 8080.

Tip

flutter_rust_bridge_codegen generate --watch regenerates the bindings each time you save a Rust file.

docs.title: Things that are generated
docs.text:
Do not edit these by hand; regenerate them.

Path Regenerate with tms_client/lib/generated/** ./run_codegen tms_infra/src/frb_generated.rs ./run_codegen tms_client/web/pkg/** ./run_codegen echo_tree_flutter/rust_schemas/echoTreeSchema.json Any build of echo_tree_infra

docs.title: Hiding Rust items from the bridge
docs.text:
Everything public under tms_infra::infra is exposed to Dart by default. Mark items that only the server needs so that no bindings are generated for them:

#[flutter_rust_bridge::frb(ignore)]
fn to_schema() -> String { /* server only */ }

The season structs and the JSON schema functions are already marked this way.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
The GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/ci.yml generates the bindings, builds the wasm module, builds the client for each platform and the server for each operating system, and publishes release artefacts. The Flutter and codegen versions it installs are pinned in the env block at the top of that file. Keep them in step with the versions on this page.

Pushes to master and ci-cd also release: a draft GitHub release for the version in vars.yml, the Docker image, and the TestFlight build. The draft is published by hand. Once a version is published, later pushes build but do not release until tms_version is bumped.

This documentation is built by .github/workflows/gh-pages.yml with mkdocs build and published to GitHub Pages on pushes to master.

To preview it locally:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Testing and quality checks
docs.text: Run these before opening a pull request. They are quick, and they are what keeps the project clean.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
# Rust
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace

# Dart
cd tms_client
flutter analyze
flutter test
cd ../echo_tree_flutter
flutter analyze

All of them should finish with no warnings and no failures.

docs.title: Lints
docs.text:
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings

The workspace is kept free of clippy warnings, so -D warnings turns any new one into a failure. A small number of lints are silenced with #[allow(...)] at the exact place they apply, with the reason obvious from context. Prefer fixing a lint to silencing it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Test What it covers tms_infra/tests/fll_scoring.rs Scoring and validation for each season: defaults, every rule, every check, maximum scores, and that mission images exist echo_tree_rs backup_manager tests That a backup survives being written and read back 
cargo test --workspace

docs.title: Analyzer
docs.text:
flutter analyze

Lint rules come from flutter_lints, configured in analysis_options.yaml. Generated code under lib/generated is excluded from linting.

Because it is excluded, also check the generated code for real errors after regenerating the bridge:

dart analyze lib/generated | grep "error -"

No output means no errors.

docs.title: Bridge tests
docs.text:
tms_client/test/bridge_test.dart calls the Rust code through the bridge, natively. It checks that the seasons are present, that default answers score and validate correctly, that 2026 mission images exist, and that JSON survives a round trip.

It needs the host library, so build that first:

cargo build -p tms_infra --release
cd tms_client
flutter test

If the library has not been built, the tests are skipped with a message saying so.

docs.title: Checking the whole thing by hand
docs.text:
Automated tests do not cover the user interface. After any change that touches the client or the API, run a short end-to-end check.

flowchart LR
    A[run_codegen] --> B[flutter build web]
    B --> C[cargo run -p tms_server]
    C --> D[Log in as admin]
    D --> E[Import a sample schedule]
    E --> F[Select a season]
    F --> G[Score a sheet as a referee]
    G --> H[Check scoreboard and dashboard]

Sample schedules are in test_imports/:

File Use single_day.csv A normal single-day event multi_day.csv A multi-day event with practice matches broken_single_day.csv A schedule with deliberate mistakes, for exercising the integrity checks

A reasonable smoke test:

  • Home screen loads and the connection markers clear
  • Log in as admin
  • Import single_day.csv; the Dashboard shows the matches and no errors
  • Select a season; Referee Scoring shows that season's scoresheet with images
  • Load, ready and start a match from the Match Controller; the timer runs on the public Timer screen
  • Submit a scoresheet; the Scoreboard updates
  • Submit an impossible scoresheet; it is rejected with a message
  • Create and restore a backup

docs.title: When you change a dependency
docs.text:
• flutter_rust_bridge: the crate version in tms_infra/Cargo.toml, the package version in tms_client/pubspec.yaml, the installed flutter_rust_bridge_codegen, and the pipeline's pinned version must all be the same.
  • bincode: the backup format depends on it. A change of version or configuration makes existing backup files unreadable.
  • freezed: regenerate the bridge and check lib/generated for errors, since the generated classes depend on it.
  • Anything in tms_infra: run ./run_codegen, because the client is built from it.

docs.title: Connecting a device
docs.text:
Every device uses the same client. You can run it in a web browser or as the tablet app.

Web browseriPad or iPhoneAndroid

Open the server's address in a browser, for example http://192.168.1.20:8080. The server sends you to /ui, where the client loads.

The web client finds the server by itself, because it was loaded from it.

Install the TMS client from the App Store.

The app does not know where your server is, so the first time you open it go to the connection page (the cog icon in the top right) and enter the server's IP address and port.

Use the web client in the tablet's browser, or install the Android build from the releases page if one is published for your version.

docs.title: The connection page
docs.text:
Select the cog icon in the top right corner at any time to open the connection page. It shows:

  • the current status and the address the client is connected to,
  • fields for the Server IP Address and Server Port, with a Connect button, and
  • the client's version and build number.

docs.title: Sharing the address with a QR code
docs.text: The connection page has a QR button in the bottom right corner. Select it to show a QR code for the web client of the server this device is connected to. Another device can scan it with its camera to open TMS without typing the address.

docs.title: The connection status indicator
docs.text:
While the client is not fully connected, the top bar shows three markers in square brackets:

[OK|DC|DC]
Position What it is Meaning when it says DC First Server The server cannot be reached at all Second Live updates The live connection for match and timer events is down Third Event data The live copy of the event data is down

When all three are connected the indicator disappears. It is normal to see it for a second or two when the client starts or after a device wakes from sleep.

If it stays, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Logging in and out
docs.text:
• Select the login button in the top right corner and enter your username and password.
  • When you are logged in, the same button shows a person icon. Select it to log out.

The home screen then shows the screens available to your role. The arrow on the left edge of most screens opens a side menu with the rest.

Light and dark mode

The sun icon in the top bar switches between light and dark themes. The choice is remembered on that device.

docs.title: Event day walkthrough
docs.text: This page shows how the roles fit together across a typical day. Each role has its own detailed guide; this is the overview you can use for a volunteer briefing.

docs.title: Before teams arrive
docs.text: Who What Event administrator Start the server, import the schedule, choose the season, create accounts. See the quick start. Event administrator Open the Dashboard and clear any integrity messages. Screen and AV operator Put the Scoreboard and Timer on the venue screens, assign each timer to its tables, and connect one timer computer to the sound system. Head referee Check the Tables and Matches pages match the room. Referees Log in on each tablet, open Referee Scoring, select the table and enter a referee name. Judge advisor Check Judging Sessions and Pods.

docs.title: Running a match
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Head referee loads the next match] --> B[Queuer checks teams in]
    B --> C[Referee tablets show each table as ready]
    C --> D[Head referee readies the match]
    D --> E[Head referee or emcee starts the timer]
    E --> F[Match runs: start, end-game and end sounds]
    F --> G[Referees score with the team and submit]
    G --> H[Scoreboard and rankings update]
    H --> A
  1. The head referee loads the match in the Match Controller. The teams appear on each referee's tablet and on the emcee's Match Announcer.
  2. The queuer checks each team in as it arrives at its table.
  3. Each referee has Referee Scoring open on their table. The tablet reports to the head referee automatically, so the Match Controller shows each table as ready.
  4. The head referee readies the match, then starts the timer, either immediately or with a countdown.
  5. When the timer reaches zero the match is marked complete.
  6. Each referee completes the scoresheet with the team and submits it, and the scoreboard updates.

docs.title: During the day
docs.text:
• The judge advisor watches the Teams and Team Data pages, corrects any scores that were entered wrongly, and keeps judging sessions up to date.
  • The event administrator keeps an eye on the Dashboard. New integrity messages mean something needs attention, for example a match marked complete with no score.
  • The server takes a backup every ten minutes by default.

docs.title: When something changes
docs.text:
Schedules change. TMS is built for that:

  • A team is late or swaps a slot: the head referee can reschedule a team to another match from the Match Controller, or edit the match on the Matches page.
  • A table breaks: the head referee can move teams to another table, or remove the table.
  • A score was entered against the wrong team or round: the judge advisor can edit or delete the scoresheet from the Teams page.
  • A team withdraws: the referee submits a No Show for that round.

docs.title: At the end of the day
docs.text:
1. The judge advisor exports the results from Team Data.
  2. The event administrator creates a final backup from the Backups page and downloads it.
  3. Stop the server. Keep the server folder, or at least the downloaded backup, as your record of the event.

docs.title: How TMS works
docs.text:
TMS has two parts: one server and any number of clients.

The server is a single program that you run on a laptop or small computer at the venue. It stores the event, enforces who is allowed to do what, calculates scores and rankings, and sends every change to every connected device straight away.

A client is what people actually use. It is the same application everywhere: in a web browser, or as the tablet app. What a person sees depends on the account they log in with.

flowchart LR
    subgraph venue [Venue network]
        server[(TMS server)]
        ref1[Referee tablet]
        ref2[Referee tablet]
        hr[Head referee laptop]
        ja[Judge advisor laptop]
        board[Scoreboard screen]
        timer[Timer screen]
    end
    ref1 <--> server
    ref2 <--> server
    hr <--> server
    ja <--> server
    server --> board
    server --> timer

docs.title: Key ideas
docs.text: Everything is live There is no refresh button. When a referee submits a score, the scoreboard, the dashboard and the team pages update on their own within a moment. The server is the source of truth Devices show a copy of the event. If a tablet loses its connection it reconnects and catches up. Scores are calculated and checked again on the server, so a device cannot submit an invalid scoresheet. Roles decide what you can do Each account has one or more roles such as referee or judge advisor. The home screen and the side menu only show the screens that role is allowed to use. See Roles at a glance. No internet required Clients talk to the server over the local network. Internet access is only needed to download TMS in the first place, or if you choose to use remote access.

docs.title: The pieces of an event
docs.text:
Piece What it is Who looks after it Teams Team number, name and affiliation Judge advisor Tables The robot game tables, by name Head referee Matches Which teams play on which tables, and when Head referee Scoresheets One per team per round, submitted by a referee Referees, corrected by the judge advisor Judging pods The judging rooms, by name Judge advisor Judging sessions Which teams are in which pod, and when Judge advisor Season Which game's scoresheet the referees see Event administrator

Most of this arrives in one step when the administrator imports the schedule file.

docs.title: The public screens
docs.text:
Two screens need no login and are designed to be left running on a projector or television:

  • the Scoreboard, which shows team rankings and scores per round, and
  • the Timer, which shows the match clock and plays the start, end-game and end sounds.

See the Screen and AV operator guide.

docs.title: A match from start to finish
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Queuer
    participant R as Referees
    participant H as Head referee
    participant S as Server
    participant P as Public screens
    H->>S: Load match
    S-->>R: Match and team appear on each table
    Q->>S: Check teams in
    R-->>S: Tablets report their table is ready
    H->>S: Ready match, then Start
    S-->>P: Timer counts down with sounds
    S-->>H: Timer ends, match marked complete
    R->>S: Submit scoresheets
    S-->>P: Scoreboard updates

Next: set up an event.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page takes you from a fresh download to an event that is ready for referees. Allow about ten minutes.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • a computer to run the server, connected to the venue network,
  • the schedule file for your event, exported from the FLL scheduler as a CSV file (see Schedules), and
  • a device with a web browser.

docs.title: 1. Start the server
docs.text:
1. Download the build for your platform from the releases page and unpack it somewhere you can find again.
  2. Run tms_server from inside the unpacked folder.

The server prints the address it is hosting on, for example http://192.168.1.20:8080. Keep the window open for the whole event.

Tip

Run the server from its own folder. It keeps its database, backups and logs next to the program. See Installing the server for Docker and the other options.

docs.title: 2. Open the client
docs.text:
On any device on the same network, open a browser and go to the address the server printed. You are taken to /ui, the TMS client.

The top bar shows a connection status while the client finds the server. When it disappears, you are connected. If it does not, see Connecting a device.

docs.title: 3. Log in as the administrator
docs.text:
Select the login button in the top right corner and sign in with:

Username Password admin admin

Change the admin password

Anyone on the network can use the default password. Change it in the next step.

docs.title: 4. Set up the event
docs.text:
From the home screen open Setup. Each row has its own send button; nothing is saved until you press it.

  1. Set admin password: choose a new password and send it.
  2. Set event name: optional.
  3. Upload schedule: choose your CSV file, then send it. This creates the teams, tables, matches, judging pods and judging sessions.
  4. Select Blueprint: choose the season your event is running, for example 2026-Founders, and send it. See Seasons and games.

The remaining options (timer lengths and backup settings) have sensible defaults. They are described in Event setup.

docs.title: 5. Create accounts for your volunteers
docs.text:
1. Open the side menu with the arrow on the left edge of the screen and choose Users.
  2. Select Add default users to create one account for each common role.
Username Password Role head_referee head_referee Head referee referee referee Referee judge_advisor judge_advisor Judge advisor judge judge Judge

Change the passwords or add your own accounts as needed. See Users and passwords.

docs.title: 6. Check the event
docs.text:
Open Dashboard from the home screen. You should see:

  • the number of matches, judging sessions and expected scores, and
  • an Integrity Messages panel. If it lists anything, the schedule has a problem worth fixing before teams arrive. See Integrity checks.

docs.title: You are ready
docs.text:
• Server running
  • Admin password changed
  • Schedule imported
  • Season selected
  • Volunteer accounts created

Hand each volunteer the page for their role from Roles at a glance, and read the Event day walkthrough for how the day fits together.

docs.title: Integrity checks
docs.text: TMS continuously checks the event data for mistakes: a team scheduled twice, a score that was never submitted, a match on a table that does not exist. Anything it finds is shown as an integrity message with a code.

docs.title: Where messages appear
docs.text:
Screen Shows Dashboard Every message for the whole event Matches An icon on each match with a problem, and counts in the banner Teams The issues for the selected team Judging Sessions An icon on each session with a problem, and counts in the banner

The server re-checks the event every ten seconds. Messages clear by themselves when the cause is fixed.

docs.title: Errors and warnings
docs.text: Errors (E) Something is wrong and will affect results or the running of the event. Fix these. Warnings (W) Something looks unusual. Many warnings are normal for a short time during the day, such as a match that has just finished and has not been scored yet.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Code Message What to do E001 Team number is missing Give the team a number on the Teams page. E002 Duplicate team number Two teams share a number. Correct or delete one. E003 Team has conflicting scores A team has two scoresheets for one round. The judge advisor deletes or re-rounds one. E004 Table does not exist in event A match uses a table name that is not on the Tables page. Add the table or fix the match. E005 Team in match does not exist in this event A match lists a team number that is not on the Teams page. Fix the match or add the team. E006 Duplicate match number Two matches share a number. Renumber one. E007 Team has fewer matches than the maximum number of rounds One team is scheduled for fewer matches than the others. Add it to a match. E008 Pod does not exist in event A session uses a pod name that is not on the Pods page. E009 Team in pod does not exist in this event A session lists a team number that is not on the Teams page. E010 Team has more than one judging session Remove the team from the extra session. E011 Team is not in any judging sessions Add the team to a session. E012 Duplicate session number Renumber one of the sessions. E013 Team has match overlapping with judging session Move the match or the session. E000 Unknown error Check the server log and report it.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text: Code Message What it usually means W001 Team name is missing The team has a number but no name. W002 Duplicate team name Two teams have the same name. Often fine. W003 Team has a round 0 score A scoresheet was submitted without a real round. Move it to the right round. W004 No tables or teams found in match An empty match. Delete it or fill it in. W005 Match is complete but score not submitted A referee has not submitted yet, or a no-show was not recorded. W006 Match is not complete but score submitted A score exists for a match that was never run on the timer. Mark the match completed if it was played. W007 Blank table in match A match has a team with no table name. W008 No team on table A table in a match has no team. W009 Team has judging session within 10 minutes of match A tight turnaround. Warn the team or move one of them. W010 No pods or teams found in sessions An empty session. W011 Session complete, but no core values score submitted The Core Values tick is missing for a finished session. W012 Session complete, but no innovation score submitted The Innovation tick is missing for a finished session. W013 Session complete, but no robot design score submitted The Robot Design tick is missing for a finished session. W014 Session not complete, but core values score submitted A rubric was ticked for a session that has not happened yet. W015 Session not complete, but innovation score submitted As above, for Innovation. W016 Session not complete, but robot design score submitted As above, for Robot Design. W017 Blank pod in session A session has a team with no pod name. W018 No team in pod A pod in a session has no team. W000 Unknown warning Check the server log and report it.

docs.title: A sensible routine
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Import schedule] --> B{Any errors?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Fix in the scheduler and re-import, or edit in TMS]
    C --> B
    B -- No --> D[Run the event]
    D --> E[Check the Dashboard between rounds]
    E --> F{New messages?}
    F -- Yes --> G[Hand to the head referee or judge advisor]
    G --> E
    F -- No --> E
  • After importing, there should be no errors. Errors at this point come from the schedule itself.
  • During the day, expect W005 to appear briefly after each match and clear as referees submit.
  • At the end of the day, there should be no E003, W005 or W006 left. If there are, results may be incomplete.

docs.title: Rankings and the scoreboard
docs.text: TMS recalculates every team's rank each time a scoresheet is added, changed or removed. Nobody needs to press anything.

docs.title: How teams are ranked
docs.text:
Teams are ranked on their best score, the same way the official FLL robot game ranking works.

  1. Each team's scores are sorted from highest to lowest.
  2. Teams are compared on their highest score.
  3. If those are equal, they are compared on their second-highest score, then their third, and so on.
  4. Teams that are equal on every score they both have share a rank.

Example

Team Round 1 Round 2 Round 3 Best Rank A 250 310 280 310 1 B 310 200 260 310 2 C 300 305 190 305 3

A and B both have a best score of 310. A's second-best is 280 and B's is 260, so A ranks higher.

A team with no scoresheets has no rank yet.

docs.title: What counts
docs.text:
Every scoresheet a team has counts towards its ranking, including a no-show, which counts as zero.

Round 0

A scoresheet recorded against round 0 was submitted without a real round, usually because no match was loaded when the referee submitted. It still counts towards ranking. TMS raises warning W003 so the judge advisor can move the sheet to the right round or remove it.

docs.title: The scoreboard
docs.text:
The public Scoreboard shows, for every team:

  • its rank,
  • its name,
  • its best score, and
  • its score in each round.

A round with no score yet shows ?. A round with more than one scoresheet shows Conflict until the judge advisor resolves it; see Conflicting scores.

The number of round columns grows as rounds are played.

Optional panels, switched on with the tick boxes at the top, show the upcoming match schedule and judging schedule. See the screen and AV operator guide.

docs.title: Hiding scores late in the day
docs.text: Some events stop showing live scores before the final round so that results are a surprise at the ceremony. TMS has no switch for this. The simplest way is to take the scoreboard off the public screens, or show the Timer instead, for the final round.

docs.title: Getting the final results
docs.text: The judge advisor exports the final table from Team Data, which includes rank and every round's score, Gracious Professionalism rating and comment. See the judge advisor guide.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text: TMS takes its teams, tables, matches, judging pods and judging sessions from one schedule file. After the import, everything can be edited by hand.

docs.title: Where the file comes from
docs.text: TMS reads the CSV file produced by the FLL tournament scheduler used by FIRST Australia: the FLL Scheduler. Build your schedule there and export it.

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
1. Log in as an admin and open Setup.
  2. Under Schedule Setup, select Select Schedule (CSV) and choose the file.
  3. Press the send button on that row.

A confirmation appears when the import succeeds. Then open the Dashboard and check the Integrity Messages panel.

Importing again

Importing a schedule into an event that already has data merges the file into what is there. It does not remove teams, matches or sessions that are missing from the new file. To replace a schedule completely, take a backup, Purge the event in Setup, then import the new file.

docs.title: What the import creates
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    csv[Schedule CSV] --> teams[Teams]
    csv --> tables[Tables]
    csv --> matches[Ranking matches]
    csv --> practice[Practice matches]
    csv --> pods[Judging pods]
    csv --> sessions[Judging sessions]
From the file Becomes in TMS Team list Teams, with number, name and affiliation Table names Tables Ranking matches Matches in the Ranking Matches category Practice matches, if present Matches in the Practice Matches category Room names Pods Judging time slots Judging sessions

docs.title: The file format
docs.text:
You do not normally need to edit the file, but it helps to know its shape when an import fails. It is a plain CSV file made of numbered blocks.

schedule.csv (shortened)
Version Number,1
Block Format,1
Number of Teams,40
1,Orion,Ardross Primary School,
2,TIE-Dye FIGHTERS,Atwell College,
...
Block Format,2
Number of Ranking Matches,60
Number of Tables,6
Number of Teams per Table,2
Number of Simultaneous Tables,1
Table Names,Red,Blue,Pink,Yellow,Green,Black,
1,10:00:00 AM,10:04:00 AM,10,28,,,,,
2,10:07:00 AM,10:11:00 AM,,,18,2,,,
...
Block Format,3
Number of Judged Events,1
Number of Event Time Slots,4
Number of Judging Teams,10
Event Name,Judging
Room Names,Pod 1,Pod 2,Pod 3,
1,10:30:00 AM,11:00:00 AM,18,27,40,
...
Block Contents Row format 1 Teams Team number, team name, affiliation 2 Ranking matches Match number, start time, end time, then one team number per table in the order of Table Names. An empty cell means that table is not used in the match. 3 Judging Session number, start time, end time, then one team number per room in the order of Room Names 4 Practice matches (optional) Same as block 2

Rules the importer applies:

  • The first line must be Version Number,1.
  • Times must be written as HH:MM:SS. They are read as 24-hour times; the AM or PM after them is ignored. Write two in the afternoon as 14:00:00.
  • For multi-day events the scheduler puts the day in front of the time. TMS keeps that text as the match's sub-category so each day's matches stay together.

docs.title: Editing after import
docs.text:
To change Who Where A team's name or affiliation Judge advisor Teams Add or remove a team Judge advisor Teams A match's time, tables or teams Head referee Matches, or the row actions in Match Controller Move one team to another match Head referee Match Controller → Reschedule Add, rename or remove a table Head referee Tables A session's time or teams Judge advisor Judging Sessions Add, rename or remove a pod Judge advisor Pods

Every change is live on every device.

docs.title: After any change
docs.text: Check the integrity messages. They exist to catch exactly the mistakes that hand edits cause: a team in two places at once, a team with one match too few, or a match on a table that no longer exists. See Integrity checks.

docs.title: If the import fails
docs.text:
Invalid version or unknown CSV type

The file does not start with Version Number,1. Make sure you exported the schedule itself and not a report, and that the file was not re-saved by a spreadsheet program in another format.

The import succeeds but times are wrong

Times are read as 24-hour. An afternoon match written as 02:00:00 PM is read as two in the morning. Re-export from the scheduler, which writes 24-hour times.

Teams or tables are missing

The counts at the top of each block (Number of Teams, Number of Tables) must match the rows and names that follow. A file edited by hand often leaves these out of step.

docs.title: Scoring and scoresheets
docs.text: This page explains how scoring works in TMS for anyone who needs more than the referee guide: how scoresheets are built, how scores are calculated and checked, and how they are corrected.

docs.title: Two ways to score
docs.text:
The event administrator chooses how referees score in Setup → Season Setup.

Season scoresheet Referees answer the questions on the season's official scoresheet. TMS calculates the score and checks the answers. This is the normal choice. Agnostic Referees type in the final score. Nothing is calculated or checked. Use this for off-season events or games TMS does not have a scoresheet for.

The available seasons are listed in Seasons and games.

docs.title: The life of a scoresheet
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Referee answers questions on the tablet] --> B[Tablet calculates score and checks answers]
    B --> C{Any problems?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Problem shown under the question, submit blocked]
    D --> A
    C -- No --> E[Referee submits]
    E --> F[Server checks and calculates again]
    F --> G{Valid?}
    G -- No --> H[Rejected with a message]
    G -- Yes --> I[Stored against team, round and table]
    I --> J[Rankings and scoreboard update]

The server never trusts the score a device sends. It recalculates the score from the answers and runs the same checks, so every device and the server always agree.

docs.title: What a scoresheet records
docs.text: Field Where it comes from Team The team scheduled on the referee's table in the loaded match Round The team's round, from the schedule Match number The loaded match Table The table the referee selected Referee The name the referee entered Answers One per question Score Calculated from the answers Gracious Professionalism 2 - Developing, 3 - Accomplished or 4 - Exceeds Private comment Free text, seen by event staff only No show Whether the team did not play Timestamp When it was submitted Modified by Set if the sheet was later corrected

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Each mission on the scoresheet has one or more questions. Every question has a fixed list of answers and a default.

  • Yes / No questions and short lists are shown as buttons.
  • Number ranges with more than eight options, such as "how many, from 0 to 50", are shown as a counter with −1 and +1 buttons. Ranges longer than twenty also get −5 and +5.

Defaults are chosen so that an untouched scoresheet is the score of a robot that never left base. For example, precision tokens default to all remaining, and "is the model still in its starting position" defaults to yes.

docs.title: How a score is calculated
docs.text:
Most answers are simply worth a number of points. Some depend on other answers:

  • a bonus that only counts if the main part of the mission was achieved,
  • a mission that scores nothing if a condition is broken, or
  • a count that is capped by another count.

TMS applies these rules for you. If you select a bonus without its condition, you get no points for it and a message explains why.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
A scoresheet cannot be submitted while it breaks one of the season's rules. Typical checks:

  • Dependent answers: a bonus is selected but the thing it depends on is not.
  • Impossible counts: more objects are recorded in a scoring area than were ever released onto the field.
  • Missing answers: a question has no answer.

The message is shown in red under the question it relates to.

Gracious Professionalism comments

Any rating other than 3 - Accomplished needs a private comment before the sheet can be submitted, so that the judges know why.

docs.title: No shows
docs.text: A referee uses No Show when a team does not play a round. The sheet is stored with a score of zero and flagged as a no-show. This keeps the event complete: the round is not reported as a missing score.

docs.title: Agnostic scoring
docs.text: In agnostic mode the scoresheet is a single Score box and a private comment. The score is stored exactly as entered. Rankings, the scoreboard and the integrity checks work in the same way.

docs.title: Correcting scores
docs.text:
Only a judge advisor (or an admin) can change a submitted scoresheet, from the team's page under Teams. They can:

  • edit the answers, round, table, referee or match number,
  • mark or unmark a no-show,
  • delete the sheet, or
  • add a sheet by hand.

Edited sheets are recalculated and checked like any other, and record who changed them. See the judge advisor guide.

docs.title: Conflicting scores
docs.text:
If a team has more than one scoresheet for the same round, TMS cannot know which is right. It:

  • shows Conflict for that round on the scoreboard, and
  • raises error E003 on the Dashboard and the team's page.

The judge advisor resolves it by deleting the wrong sheet or moving it to the correct round.

docs.title: Seasons and games
docs.text: A season in TMS is a scoresheet: the missions, questions, points and checks for one robot game. The event administrator chooses the season in Setup → Season Setup → Select Blueprint.

docs.title: Available seasons
docs.text:
Blueprint Game Notes 2026-Founders BIOGLOW, Founders edition Missions M00 to M15 plus precision tokens 2026-Future BIOGLOW, Future edition Five missions plus the Level Up Challenge 2025 UNEARTHED 2024 SUBMERGED 2023 MASTERPIECE Agnostic Any Score entry only, no scoresheet

Two games in 2026

The 2026 season has two editions of the game, played by different programs. They are separate blueprints because their fields, missions and scoresheets are different. Choose the one your event is running. An event runs one blueprint at a time.

docs.title: Changing the season
docs.text:
You can change the blueprint at any time. Scoresheets already submitted keep the season they were scored under, so their scores do not change.

Change it before referees start scoring. If the blueprint changes while a referee has a sheet open, their sheet resets to the new season's defaults.

docs.title: BIOGLOW Founders (2026-Founders)
docs.text:
Mission Name M00 Equipment Inspection Bonus M01 Drone Survey M02 Exploding Seeds M03 Flip the Rock M04 Lucky Leaves M05 Reaching Roots M06 Leafcutter Frenzy M07 Humongous Fungus M08 Tangled M09 Research Platform M10 Fragile Microhabitats M11 Window to the Past M12 Forest Elder M13 Keystone Species M14 Seeds of Renewal M15 Biocentric Architecture M16 Precision Tokens

Missions marked with a red dot on the scoresheet have no equipment constraint.

Checks the scoresheet makes for you:

  • M01: the LiDAR map bonus needs the drone to have been flown.
  • M03: the rock bonus needs the research flag to be down.
  • M04: the second leaf only scores with the katydid in its starting position, and a katydid outside the leaf habitat scores zero for the mission.
  • M06: leaf fragments only count when the ant is touching the nest.
  • M07: connection bonuses need the mycelium completely extended.
  • M14: seeds in the replantation station cannot exceed the seeds released in M02 and M09, and seeds touching the mat cannot exceed seeds in the station.
  • M15: the environmental bonus is scored when the feature matching the model's dock is complete.

docs.title: BIOGLOW Future (2026-Future)
docs.text:
Mission Name M01 Mighty Microbiomes M02 Roots of Renewal M03 Cave Waterfall M04 Rainforest Awakening M05 Central Haven (Cooperative) Level Up Invasive Attack

Several questions in this game are counts with a large range, such as the cave waterfall counter from 0 to 50. These use the counter control described in Scoring and scoresheets.

Checks the scoresheet makes for you:

  • M01: the invasive queen bonus needs three keystone species in the young forest.
  • Level Up: invasive species in the containment zone cannot exceed the number added before the match plus the queen.

docs.title: Mission images
docs.text: Each mission on the scoresheet shows a picture of its model so that referees can find the right block quickly. If a mission has no picture, the FIRST logo is shown instead.

docs.title: Official rules come first
docs.text:
TMS scoresheets follow the published robot game rules and the official scoresheet for each season. If a ruling at your event differs from what the scoresheet allows, the head referee decides, and the judge advisor can adjust a submitted sheet to match.

If you believe a scoresheet in TMS is wrong, please raise an issue with the mission and the rule reference.

For developers

Adding a season is described in Adding a season.

docs.title: Match timer
docs.text: There is one match timer for the whole event. The server runs it, and every device shows the same clock.

docs.title: Who can do what
docs.text:
Action Head referee Emcee Start the match Start with a countdown Abort a running match

The timer can only be started when a match is loaded and ready. See the head referee guide.

docs.title: Timer phases
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Countdown: Countdown
    Idle --> Running: Start
    Countdown --> Running: Countdown ends
    Running --> Endgame: End-game time reached
    Endgame --> Ended: Clock reaches zero
    Running --> Stopped: Abort
    Endgame --> Stopped: Abort
    Ended --> Idle: Resets after a moment
    Stopped --> Idle: Resets after a moment
Phase What you see and hear Idle The clock shows the full match length Countdown A short countdown, with a beep each second Running The clock counts down. A start sound plays at the beginning. End-game The clock changes colour. An end-game sound plays once. Ended The clock is at zero. An end sound plays. The loaded matches are marked complete and unloaded. Stopped The head referee aborted. A stop sound plays. The match is not marked complete and stays ready.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Set by the event administrator in Setup → Game Scoring Setup.

Setting Default Meaning Timer length 150 seconds The length of a match (2:30) Endgame length 30 seconds How long before the end the end-game phase begins

Changes apply from the next match.

docs.title: Where the timer appears
docs.text:
Screen Shows the clock Plays the sounds Timer (public) Scoreboard (public), with the match schedule shown Match Controller Match Announcer Dashboard

Getting sound into the room

Connect one computer showing the Timer to the sound system. Every other device that has a sound-playing screen open will play the sounds too, so mute those, or the room hears each sound several times.

Browsers and automatic sound

Browsers do not play sound on a page until someone has clicked or tapped on it, and may stop again if the page is left untouched for a long time.

Interact with the page once after opening it. For a device that will play sound all day in Chrome or Edge, also allow sound permanently: select the icon to the left of the address, open Site settings, and set Sound to Allow. This is remembered per server address.

docs.title: If the timer and the room disagree
docs.text:
Every device counts from messages sent by the server once a second, so screens stay in step even on a slow network. A device that was disconnected during a match shows the correct time as soon as it reconnects.

If a screen is frozen, reload the page. This never affects the match itself; the timer runs on the server.

docs.title: Roles at a glance
docs.text: Every TMS account has one or more roles. A role decides which screens appear on the home screen and in the side menu, and what the server will accept from that account.

docs.title: Which guide should I read?
docs.text: If you are... Read Setting up the server and the event Event administrator Running matches and the timer Head referee Scoring at a table Referee Getting teams to their tables on time Queuer Announcing matches Emcee Looking after teams, judging and results Judge advisor Judging teams Judge Looking after the venue screens and sound Screen and AV operator

docs.title: What each role can open
docs.text: Screen Admin Head referee Referee Queuer Emcee Judge advisor No login Scoreboard Timer Referee Scoring Match Controller Matches Tables Match Announcer Queueing Teams Team Data Judging Sessions Pods Setup Dashboard Users Backups

docs.title: How roles combine
docs.text:
• Admin can do everything.
  • Head referee includes everything a referee and a queuer can do.
  • Judge advisor includes everything a judge can do.
  • An account can hold several roles at once. For example, a head referee who also announces can be given the emcee role too.
flowchart TD
    admin[Admin] --> hr[Head referee]
    admin --> ja[Judge advisor]
    admin --> emcee[Emcee]
    hr --> ref[Referee]
    hr --> queuer[Queuer]
    ja --> judge[Judge]

docs.title: Who can change what
docs.text:
Action Role required Submit a scoresheet Referee Edit or delete a scoresheet Judge advisor Load, ready and edit matches Head referee Start the timer Head referee or emcee Stop (abort) the timer Head referee Add or remove tables Head referee Check a team in Queuer Add, edit or remove teams Judge advisor Edit judging sessions and pods Judge advisor Event setup, users and backups Admin

Roles without their own screens
